results.summary: This design implements a Simon Says memory game where the player must repeat an ever-growing sequence of colors and tones. The sequence is shown on four LEDs with corresponding tones on a speaker, and the player responds using four buttons. A two-digit seven-segment display shows the current level, and the game restarts after a mistake. It requires external hardware such as the Simon Says Pmod or discrete buttons, LEDs, a speaker, and a seven-segment display, and a Wokwi simulation is available.

This analog design generates a stepwise approximation of a sine wave, with the output frequency depending on the clock. It is intended as a sine wave synthesizer and uses analog pins for bias and current outputs. Testing requires a 1 kΩ resistor from the output pins to ground. The documentation is brief and does not provide detailed specifications or test results.

This design implements a 16-microphone delay-and-sum beamformer that processes PDM input from up to 16 digital microphones. It converts the PDM data to PCM using a 3-stage CIC filter and outputs the result as an I2S stream. The design requires external digital microphones, a clock generator, and an I2S receiver. It is notable for its high channel count and integrated filtering.

This design implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game with VGA output. The player uses four buttons to move tiles in four directions, merging matching numbers to reach 2048. It includes a debug mode for unit testing and requires a TinyVGA Pmod for display. Silicon testing confirmed it works, with a tester successfully playing a game.

This design is a 4-bit carry look-ahead adder that computes the sum of two 4-bit inputs plus a carry-in. It provides sum and carry-out outputs and can be used as a building block for larger adders. The design was tested on an FPGA but has no silicon test report. The documentation is minimal but sufficient to understand its function.

This design is an ASIC implementation of a university CPLD project that drives four multiplexed seven-segment displays and scans a multiplexed keypad. It uses a simple SPI protocol to receive commands for display data and keypad column selection, and it outputs keypad row data on MISO. The design requires external hardware including displays, a keypad, and an SPI master, and it must be clocked by the SPI clock. Silicon testing showed it functional up to 3.7 MHz, but auto-clocking must be disabled.

This design is a tiny system-on-chip featuring a 16-bit microprocessor, boot ROM, PWM, timer, and SPI interface. The CPU runs a built-in program that reads from an 8-bit input port and writes to an 8-bit output port, and it also exercises the SPI, PWM, and timer peripherals. The design is intended to test the microprocessor on silicon and requires external hardware such as a keypad and display. The documentation is detailed but the external hardware is not fully specified.

This design plays Pachelbel's Canon while displaying synchronized visuals on a VGA screen. It uses a PWM output for audio and requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a Tiny Audio Pmod. Silicon testing showed it works, though one tester noted the audio was out of sync until manually reset. The design is a demonstration of audio and video capabilities on Tiny Tapeout.

This design computes and displays the Mandelbrot fractal on a VGA screen using a racing-the-beam technique. It uses 16-bit fixed-point arithmetic and a maximum iteration depth of 14, with configurable position and zoom via input pins. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a 100 MHz clock. Silicon testing showed it broadly works, though the demo mode can sometimes get stuck zooming into the wrong offset.

This design displays a static image of a plane flying into the sunset with a text overlay that types out character by character. It also includes demos for oscilloscope XY display PMODs, which can be selected via input pins. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod for the main demo and additional PMODs for the XY demos. The text animation may complete before the VGA monitor recognizes the signal, so viewing in a VGA playground is recommended.
